modules.title: 9.1 Nitrogen, the Nitrogen Cycle, Ammonia and HNO3
modules.html:
Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere by volume yet plants cannot use it directly, because the \(N\equiv N\) triple bond has a bond energy of about \(945\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\) — one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. This inertness explains both nitrogen's uses and the need for the nitrogen cycle.

Preparation and properties of nitrogen

  • Industrially: fractional distillation of liquid air (nitrogen boils off first at \(-196^{\circ}C\)).
  • Laboratory: gently heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and sodium nitrite: \(NH_4Cl + NaNO_2 \rightarrow NaCl + 2H_2O + N_2\). Alternatively, air is passed over hot copper to remove oxygen, then through \(NaOH\) to remove \(CO_2\).
  • Colourless, odourless, slightly less dense than air, sparingly soluble, neutral to litmus.
  • Reacts only under extreme conditions: with hydrogen (Haber process), with oxygen in lightning or a car engine (\(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\)), and with heated magnesium (\(3Mg + N_2 \rightarrow Mg_3N_2\), whose hydrolysis liberates ammonia).
  • Uses: filling electric bulbs and food packets (inert atmosphere), liquid nitrogen as a refrigerant, and manufacture of ammonia and fertilisers.

The nitrogen cycle

  1. Nitrogen fixation: by lightning (\(N_2 \rightarrow NO \rightarrow NO_2 \rightarrow HNO_3\) washed down as rain), by Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of legumes, and industrially by the Haber process.
  2. Nitrification: soil bacteria oxidise ammonium salts to nitrites (Nitrosomonas) and nitrites to nitrates (Nitrobacter).
  3. Assimilation: plants absorb nitrates and build proteins; animals get nitrogen by eating plants.
  4. Ammonification: decay bacteria convert dead matter and excreta back to ammonia.
  5. Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria return nitrates to atmospheric \(N_2\), closing the cycle.

Ammonia, \(NH_3\)

Manufacture (Haber process): \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3;\ \Delta H = -92\ kJ\,mol^{-1}\), at about \(450^{\circ}C\), \(200\ atm\), with finely divided iron catalyst promoted by \(K_2O\) and \(Al_2O_3\). The moderate temperature is a compromise: a lower temperature would give a higher yield (exothermic, Le Chatelier) but too slow a rate.

Laboratory: heat any ammonium salt with an alkali, \(2NH_4Cl + Ca(OH)_2 \rightarrow CaCl_2 + 2H_2O + 2NH_3\); dry with quicklime (never \(H_2SO_4\) or \(CaCl_2\), which react with it) and collect by upward delivery because it is less dense than air.

Properties: pungent, extremely soluble (fountain experiment), the only common alkaline gas — it turns damp red litmus blue. Dense white fumes of \(NH_4Cl\) form with \(HCl\) (a standard test). It burns in oxygen only over a catalyst; it reduces heated copper(II) oxide: \(3CuO + 2NH_3 \rightarrow 3Cu + N_2 + 3H_2O\). Aqueous ammonia precipitates metal hydroxides and dissolves \(Cu^{2+}\) in excess to a deep-blue complex, \(Cu(NH_3)_4^{2+}\).

Trioxonitrate(V) acid, \(HNO_3\)

Ostwald process: \(4NH_3 + 5O_2 \xrightarrow{Pt, 900^{\circ}C} 4NO + 6H_2O\); \(2NO + O_2 \rightarrow 2NO_2\); \(4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 4HNO_3\).

It is a strong acid, a powerful oxidising agent (it oxidises copper, sulphur and carbon) and it is photosensitive, so it is stored in dark bottles: \(4HNO_3 \rightarrow 4NO_2 + O_2 + 2H_2O\). With copper: dilute acid gives \(NO\), concentrated acid gives brown \(NO_2\). Concentrated \(HNO_3\) renders iron and aluminium passive by forming an oxide film. Heating a trioxonitrate(V) salt gives characteristic products: \(NaNO_3 \rightarrow NaNO_2 + O_2\), while \(2Cu(NO_3)_2 \rightarrow 2CuO + 4NO_2 + O_2\).
examples: Explain why the Haber process uses 450 C rather than a much lower temperature.
Write equations for the three stages of the Ostwald process.

modules.title: 9.2 Sulphur and its Compounds
modules.html:
Sulphur is a yellow, brittle, insoluble-in-water solid that occurs free in volcanic regions and combined as sulphides and sulphates. It shows allotropy: rhombic (\(\alpha\)) sulphur is stable below \(96^{\circ}C\), monoclinic (\(\beta\)) sulphur above it; \(96^{\circ}C\) is the transition temperature. Plastic sulphur is formed when molten sulphur is poured into cold water.

Chemical properties of sulphur

  • Burns in air with a blue flame: \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\).
  • With metals: \(Fe + S \rightarrow FeS\); \(2Cu + S \rightarrow Cu_2S\).
  • With hot concentrated acids: \(S + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 3SO_2 + 2H_2O\); \(S + 6HNO_3 \rightarrow H_2SO_4 + 6NO_2 + 2H_2O\).
  • Uses: vulcanising rubber, making \(H_2SO_4\), gunpowder, fungicides, matches and drugs.

Sulphur(IV) oxide, \(SO_2\)

Preparation: \(Na_2SO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O + SO_2\), or by burning sulphur. It is a colourless gas with a choking smell, denser than air, very soluble giving trioxosulphate(IV) acid \(H_2SO_3\).

  • Acidic oxide: turns damp blue litmus red.
  • Reducing agent: decolourises acidified \(KMnO_4\) (purple to colourless) and turns orange \(K_2Cr_2O_7\) green — the standard tests. It also bleaches by reduction, so the bleached article slowly regains colour in air, unlike chlorine's permanent oxidative bleaching.
  • Used to preserve food, fumigate, bleach straw and wool, and make \(H_2SO_4\).

Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid and the Contact process

  1. \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\) (sulphur or roasted sulphide ore burned in dry air).
  2. \(2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3;\ \Delta H = -196\ kJ\), at \(450^{\circ}C\), 2 atm, over vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
  3. \(SO_3\) is absorbed in concentrated \(H_2SO_4\) to give oleum, \(H_2S_2O_7\), which is then diluted: \(H_2S_2O_7 + H_2O \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4\). Direct absorption in water is avoided because it produces an uncontrollable acid mist.

Properties of the concentrated acid:

  • Dibasic strong acid when dilute: \(H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O\).
  • Dehydrating agent: it chars sugar (\(C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} \rightarrow 12C + 11H_2O\)) and turns blue \(CuSO_4\!\cdot\!5H_2O\) white.
  • Oxidising agent when hot and concentrated: \(Cu + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + SO_2 + 2H_2O\).
  • Non-volatile, so it displaces volatile acids from their salts: \(NaCl + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow NaHSO_4 + HCl\).
  • Test for the sulphate ion: add dilute \(HCl\) then \(BaCl_2\); a white precipitate of \(BaSO_4\) insoluble in excess acid confirms \(SO_4^{2-}\).
  • Safety: always add the acid to water, never water to acid — dilution is strongly exothermic.

Hydrogen sulphide, \(H_2S\)

Prepared from iron(II) sulphide and dilute \(HCl\): \(FeS + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2S\). It is a poisonous gas smelling of rotten eggs, a weak acid in water and a strong reducing agent; it turns lead(II) ethanoate paper black (\(PbS\)) — the standard test — and precipitates coloured metal sulphides used in qualitative analysis.
examples: Distinguish between the bleaching action of SO2 and that of chlorine.
State three properties of concentrated H2SO4 with an equation for each.

modules.title: 9.3 The Halogens
modules.html:
The halogens (Group 17: F, Cl, Br, I, At) each have seven outer electrons and need only one more to complete the octet, so they are the most reactive non-metals and never occur free in nature. They exist as diatomic molecules and form salts (halides) with metals — the name means "salt-former".

Trends down the group

PropertyF → I
Physical statePale-yellow gas → green-yellow gas → red-brown liquid → grey-black solid
Colour intensityDeepens down the group
Melting/boiling pointIncreases (larger molecules, stronger van der Waals forces)
Electronegativity and reactivityDecreases — the atom gets larger so the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly
Oxidising powerDecreases: \(F_2 > Cl_2 > Br_2 > I_2\)
Stability of hydride\(HF > HCl > HBr > HI\)

Displacement: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: \(Cl_2 + 2KBr \rightarrow 2KCl + Br_2\) (solution turns orange-brown); \(Cl_2 + 2KI \rightarrow 2KCl + I_2\) (brown solution, black solid).

Chlorine

Laboratory preparation: oxidation of concentrated hydrochloric acid by manganese(IV) oxide on heating, \(MnO_2 + 4HCl \rightarrow MnCl_2 + 2H_2O + Cl_2\), or at room temperature with \(KMnO_4\). The gas is passed through water (removes \(HCl\) fumes), then concentrated \(H_2SO_4\) (dries it) and collected by downward delivery.

Industrially it is a product of the electrolysis of concentrated brine, with \(NaOH\) and \(H_2\) as co-products.

Properties: green-yellow, choking, poisonous, denser than air, moderately soluble giving chlorine water, a mixture of \(HCl\) and \(HOCl\). The \(HOCl\) slowly releases oxygen, so chlorine bleaches by oxidation and the bleaching is permanent. Chlorine reacts directly with most metals (\(2Fe + 3Cl_2 \rightarrow 2FeCl_3\)), with hydrogen explosively in sunlight, and with cold dilute \(NaOH\) to give bleach: \(Cl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaOCl + H_2O\). With hot concentrated alkali it gives the chlorate(V): \(3Cl_2 + 6NaOH \rightarrow 5NaCl + NaClO_3 + 3H_2O\).

Uses: water sterilisation, bleaching textiles and paper, making \(HCl\), PVC, insecticides and antiseptics.

Hydrogen chloride and hydrochloric acid

Prepared by warming sodium chloride with concentrated \(H_2SO_4\); it is a colourless gas fuming in moist air, extremely soluble (fountain experiment), and its solution is a strong monobasic acid. Test for chloride ion: add dilute \(HNO_3\) then \(AgNO_3\); a white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia is \(AgCl\); a cream precipitate sparingly soluble in ammonia is \(AgBr\); a yellow precipitate insoluble in ammonia is \(AgI\).

Bromine and iodine

Bromine is a dense red-brown fuming liquid obtained from sea water and bromide brines; it is used in silver bromide photographic film and in flame retardants. Iodine is a grey-black solid that sublimes to a violet vapour; it gives a deep blue-black colour with starch (the classic test), and is used as a tincture antiseptic; iodine deficiency causes goitre, so table salt is iodised.
examples: Explain the trend in reactivity from fluorine to iodine.
Describe how you would distinguish between solutions of KCl, KBr and KI.

modules.title: 9.4 Tests, Industrial Summary and Calculations
modules.html:
This module consolidates the SSS 3 non-metal chemistry into identification tests, industrial comparisons and worked calculations of the type set in WAEC, NECO and JAMB.

Summary of industrial processes

ProcessProductCatalyst / conditions
Haber\(NH_3\)Fe with \(K_2O\)/\(Al_2O_3\); 450°C; 200 atm
Ostwald\(HNO_3\)Pt-Rh gauze; 900°C
Contact\(H_2SO_4\)\(V_2O_5\); 450°C; 2 atm
Electrolysis of brine\(Cl_2, NaOH, H_2\)Diaphragm or membrane cell

Diagnostic tests you must know

  • \(NH_3\): damp red litmus turns blue; white fumes with concentrated \(HCl\).
  • \(NO_2\): brown, choking, acidic; turns starch-iodide paper blue-black.
  • \(SO_2\): choking; decolourises acidified \(KMnO_4\) and turns \(K_2Cr_2O_7\) from orange to green.
  • \(H_2S\): rotten-egg smell; blackens lead(II) ethanoate paper.
  • \(Cl_2\): green-yellow; bleaches damp litmus permanently.
  • \(SO_4^{2-}\): white precipitate with \(BaCl_2\) after acidifying with \(HCl\).
  • \(Cl^-, Br^-, I^-\): white, cream and yellow precipitates with \(AgNO_3\) respectively.
  • \(NO_3^-\): brown-ring test with iron(II) sulphate and concentrated \(H_2SO_4\).

Worked example 1 — Haber process yield

Calculate the mass of ammonia produced when \(60\ dm^3\) of nitrogen reacts completely with hydrogen at s.t.p. (\(N=14, H=1\)).

\(n(N_2) = 60/22.4 = 2.679\ mol\). From \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3\), \(n(NH_3) = 2 \times 2.679 = 5.357\ mol\).

\(m = 5.357 \times 17 = \mathbf{91.1\ g}\).

Worked example 2 — titration with \(H_2SO_4\)

\(25.0\ cm^3\) of \(0.100\ mol\,dm^{-3}\) \(NaOH\) required \(20.0\ cm^3\) of \(H_2SO_4\). Find the concentration of the acid.

\(n(NaOH) = 0.0250 \times 0.100 = 2.50\times10^{-3}\ mol\). Since \(H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O\), \(n(H_2SO_4) = 1.25\times10^{-3}\ mol\).

\(c = 1.25\times10^{-3}/0.0200 = \mathbf{0.0625\ mol\,dm^{-3}}\).

Worked example 3 — volume of \(SO_2\)

What volume of \(SO_2\) at s.t.p. is formed when 16 g of sulphur burns completely? (\(S=32\)).

\(n(S) = 16/32 = 0.5\ mol\); \(S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2\) is 1:1, so \(V = 0.5\times22.4 = \mathbf{11.2\ dm^3}\).

Common examination traps

  1. Ammonia cannot be dried with concentrated \(H_2SO_4\) or anhydrous \(CaCl_2\) — both react with it. Use quicklime.
  2. Chlorine bleaching is permanent (oxidation); \(SO_2\) bleaching is temporary (reduction).
  3. Dilute \(HNO_3\) does not give hydrogen with metals; it gives \(NO\) or \(NO_2\), because it is an oxidising acid. Very dilute acid with magnesium is the only common exception.
  4. Concentrated \(HNO_3\) passivates iron and aluminium, which is why it is transported in aluminium tankers.
  5. Always acidify with dilute \(HNO_3\) (not \(HCl\)) before adding \(AgNO_3\), or you will precipitate \(AgCl\) from the acid itself.
examples: Calculate the mass of NH3 obtained from 60 dm3 of nitrogen at s.t.p.
Describe the brown-ring test for the trioxonitrate(V) ion.

quiz.q: The transition temperature of rhombic and monoclinic sulphur is
quiz.solution: Above 96 C monoclinic sulphur is the stable form.

quiz.q: Plastic sulphur is formed when
options: molten sulphur is poured into cold water
quiz.solution: Rapid cooling traps long chains of sulphur atoms.

quiz.q: Sulphur burns in air with a
quiz.solution: Sulphur burns with a blue flame to give SO2.

quiz.q: Sulphur(IV) oxide turns acidified potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII)
quiz.solution: SO2 reduces the purple permanganate to colourless Mn2+.

quiz.q: Sulphur(IV) oxide turns orange potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI)
quiz.solution: Dichromate is reduced to green chromium(III).

quiz.q: Bleaching by SO2 is temporary because it acts by
quiz.solution: Reduced dyes are re-oxidised in air and colour returns.

quiz.q: Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is manufactured by the
quiz.solution: SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over V2O5 and absorbed in acid.

quiz.q: The catalyst in the Contact process is
quiz.solution: V2O5 is cheaper and less easily poisoned than platinum.

options: a dense acid mist would form
quiz.solution: Direct absorption in water produces an uncontrollable mist.

quiz.q: Oleum has the formula
quiz.solution: Oleum, or fuming sulphuric acid, is diluted to give H2SO4.

quiz.q: Concentrated H2SO4 chars sugar because it is
quiz.solution: It removes the elements of water, leaving carbon.

quiz.q: When diluting concentrated H2SO4 you should
options: add acid to water slowly with stirring
quiz.solution: Dilution is very exothermic; adding acid to water disperses the heat.

quiz.solution: Barium sulphate is insoluble in dilute acid.

quiz.q: Hydrogen sulphide turns lead(II) ethanoate paper
quiz.solution: Black lead(II) sulphide is formed.

quiz.q: The halogens belong to periodic group
quiz.solution: Group 17 elements have seven outer electrons.

quiz.q: Which halogen is a red-brown liquid at room temperature?
quiz.solution: Bromine is the only liquid halogen.

quiz.q: Reactivity of the halogens down the group
quiz.solution: Larger atoms attract the incoming electron less strongly.

quiz.solution: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one.

quiz.solution: Manganese(IV) oxide oxidises concentrated hydrochloric acid on heating.

quiz.solution: Basic driers would react with the acidic gas.

quiz.solution: HOCl in chlorine water releases oxygen, so bleaching is permanent.

quiz.q: Chlorine with cold dilute sodium hydroxide gives
quiz.solution: Cold dilute alkali gives the hypochlorite used as bleach.

quiz.solution: Silver chloride is white and readily soluble in ammonia.

quiz.solution: The starch-iodine complex is deep blue-black.

quiz.q: Iodine changes directly from solid to vapour; this is
quiz.solution: Iodine sublimes to a violet vapour.

quiz.q: Deficiency of iodine in the diet causes
quiz.solution: The thyroid gland enlarges without iodine for thyroxine.

quiz.q: What mass of ammonia is formed from 2 mol of nitrogen in the Haber process? (N=14, H=1)
quiz.solution: 2 mol N2 gives 4 mol NH3 = 4 x 17 = 68 g.
